lessons.title: Ponds, dams and cages
lessons.html:
What is a production system?

A production system is the way a farm keeps and grows its animals. It includes the type of tank or pond, how water comes in and goes out, and how the animals are fed.

Earth ponds

  • A pond dug into the ground and filled with water.
  • Used for tilapia and catfish in warm areas.
  • Natural food such as algae grows in the pond. The farmer can add fertiliser and pellet feed.
  • The pond is drained to harvest the fish.
  • Good: cheap to build.
  • Problems: hard to see the fish, birds and otters eat fish, oxygen can drop at night.

Farm dams

Some farmers grow fish in existing farm dams, for example trout in cold areas. The fish are often kept in cages in the dam.

Cages

  • A net bag held up by a floating frame, in a dam, lake or the sea.
  • Water flows through the net and takes away waste.
  • Good: easy to see and feed the fish, easy to harvest.
  • Problems: nets can tear and fish escape; predators; storms can damage cages; waste goes into the dam or sea.

Safety at ponds, dams and cages

  • Pond banks are slippery and steep. Walk carefully.
  • Always wear a life jacket on cages and boats.
  • Never work alone on the water. Someone must know where you are.
  • Do not go out on the water in strong wind or storms.

lessons.title: Tanks, raceways and recirculating systems
lessons.html:
Tanks

Tanks are made of plastic, fibreglass or concrete. They are often round so water swirls and waste collects in the middle, where it goes out through a drain. Tanks are used in hatcheries, for abalone and for fish.

Raceways and flow-through systems

  • A raceway is a long, narrow channel. Water flows in at one end and out at the other.
  • In a flow-through system, clean water comes in all the time from a river, spring or the sea, and used water goes out.
  • Trout farms often use raceways with cold river water.
  • Abalone farms pump sea water through their tanks.
  • The water that goes out has fish waste in it. It must be cleaned or allowed to settle before it goes back to the river, because of the National Water Act 36 of 1998.

Recirculating aquaculture systems (RAS)

In a RAS, the same water is cleaned and used again and again. Only a little new water is added.

  1. Water leaves the fish tank.
  2. A mechanical filter removes dung and leftover feed.
  3. A biological filter has good bacteria that change poisonous ammonia into less harmful substances.
  4. Air or oxygen is added.
  5. The clean water goes back to the fish.
  • Good: uses little water, can be built anywhere, temperature can be controlled.
  • Problems: expensive, needs electricity all the time, and if a pump stops the fish can die in a short time. Power cuts are a big risk, so farms need a backup generator.

lessons.title: Shellfish systems and daily work
lessons.html:
Shellfish systems

Ropes and rafts

Mussels grow on ropes hanging from rafts or long lines in the sea. Workers check the ropes, thin out mussels when they are crowded, and harvest them by pulling up the ropes.

Baskets and racks

Oysters grow in mesh baskets or bags on racks or lines. Workers shake, turn and sort them so they grow a good shape.

Land-based abalone tanks

Abalone live in shallow tanks with sea water pumped through. They hide under plates or baskets. Workers feed kelp or pellets, clean the tanks and sort abalone by size.

Comparing systems

SystemWater useCostControl
Earth pondMediumLowLow
CageUses dam or seaMediumMedium
Flow-throughHighMediumMedium
RASLowHighHigh

Your daily work in any system

  • Check that water is flowing and that pumps and aerators are working.
  • Look at the fish or shellfish. Are they eating and acting normally?
  • Feed as the feeding chart says.
  • Clean screens and filters so they do not block.
  • Check nets, pipes and tanks for holes and leaks.
  • Remove dead animals and write down how many.
  • Report problems to your supervisor straight away.

Key points

  • Production systems include ponds, cages, tanks, raceways, RAS, ropes and baskets.
  • Flow-through systems use a lot of water; RAS cleans and reuses water.
  • In a RAS, a stopped pump can kill fish quickly; backup power is needed.
  • Check pumps, aerators, filters and nets every day.
  • Always wear a life jacket and never work alone on the water.
